doc.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: From bassist to George Shearing's road manager
title: Becoming manager; Ed Fuerst as road manager; setting up offices
summary: Ed Fuerst became Shearing's road manager, Levy the manager, and they opened offices in New York as John Levy Enterprises.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: So at this point you were road manager . . .
. . . and manager? Or you were road manager and . . .?
His wife was the manager, but she was – didn’t have much to say about anything.
How did you then become the manager from . . .?
I got off the road [to perform as manager]. We got to have another road manager, so he hired Ed [Fuerst] – he hired a friend of his [George’s]. . .

Ed Fuerst. He hired Ed Fuerst, who had been like one of these groupies. He’d go on the road with us, hang out with us everywhere we played, travel with us. [If] he enjoys a certain food, he’d take George to the – he knew all the restaurants all over the country. He had money. He was well off. And he liked – he wanted to be the road manager. He turned out to be a very good road manager. He knew business, and we work well together. Ed Furst became the road manager, and I, manager. We opened offices in New York. That’s where the quintet and then John Levy Enterprises – later it was the publishing companies that we established and all of that for each one of the artists that we represented. We were in partnership with it at the very beginning, but after a while, George wasn’t involved in the managing end of it at all. That was a separate thing for me, and his thing was a separate thing.
Did you – was the transition difficult for you? Did you miss playing?

No, no. I was doing it anyway. I was the one that caused the transition and the change, because I couldn’t do both things. I had to either do one or the other. We tried finding somebody else to be the road manager to begin with. That didn’t work, and I ended up being the road manager.
So at some point then you left the tour and opened up the offices.
